text: Zero Trust never grants blanket trust just because of where something sits on the network. Microsegmentation is that principle applied directly to network design: instead of one large trusted zone where everything can freely talk to everything else, the network is broken into many small, individually secured segments, each with rules scoped as narrowly as the workload actually requires.

A perimeter-style NSG rule might allow any traffic between any two resources inside the same subnet, trusting everything inside it equally. A microsegmented rule instead names the exact source, destination, and port a workload tier is allowed to use — a web tier reaches an app tier on port 443, full stop, and nothing else is permitted by default. Same NSGs and Security Groups you already know, scoped far tighter.

This matters because of containment, not just organization. If one workload is compromised, microsegmentation is what stops an attacker from moving freely to every other workload on the same network — a pattern called lateral movement. A microsegmented network starts from deny-by-default: no traffic is allowed between segments unless a rule explicitly permits it, and that scrutiny now applies to east-west traffic moving inside the network, not just traffic crossing the firewall.

Azure Network Security Groups scope rules to a subnet or even a single network interface rather than an entire virtual network. AWS Security Groups attach per-instance and are deny-by-default and stateful. Azure's Application Security Groups go further, letting you group VMs by role — web, app, database — and write the rule against that role instead of an IP range, so it keeps working as individual machines come and go.

Picture a three-tier app, locked down tier by tier: web-to-app allowed only on port 443, app-to-database allowed only on port 1433, nothing else permitted between tiers at all. A compromised web server in that setup can only reach the one port it's allowed to use, not the entire network behind it. Next up: a different flavor of the same principle — identity itself as the new perimeter.
